How the PJDL‑302 works

This is a two-shaft multi-disc screw press. Polymer makes wet sludge clump, a slow screw drags those clumps uphill through a stack of steel rings, and the water squeezes out between the rings. What comes out the top is a damp cake you can shovel.

The path through the machine

Seven things happen in order. Tap each one to isolate it. The yellow tags are the same device names printed on the wiring drawings and stuck on the parts in the cabinet.

What the water balance looks like

10,000 Lsludge at 1% solids, carrying 100 kg of dry solids
500 kgcake at 80% moisture, still holding that 100 kg
95%of the original mass leaves as filtrate

Worked example using general figures, not a test of this unit. Published ranges for comparable presses are 10,000–50,000 mg/L feed (1–5% solids) and cake below 80% moisture. The manual pages you sent don't give feed or cake targets for this model. Your polymer, sludge type and speed settings decide the real numbers.

Rings and the back pressure plate

A belt press or filter uses cloth, and cloth blinds. This machine has no cloth. The filter is a stack of thin steel rings with hairline gaps between them, threaded onto the screw.

Fixed rings are locked in place. Moving rings sit between them and ride on the screw, so the turning thread keeps nudging them. That constant small rubbing wipes the gaps clear, which is why the screw can run for hours on sludge without a heavy backwash.

Pressure comes from two places. The thread pitch tightens and the ring gaps narrow toward the discharge end, so the material gets less and less room. Then the back pressure plate at the end restricts the exit. Its gap is the one mechanical adjustment you set yourself.

Keep that gap at 4 mm or more. The manual says a smaller gap overloads the screw body and shortens the life of the moving rings and screw shaft. At 0 mm no cake can come out. After any adjustment, tighten the plate's fixing bolts.

The drawing shows the general design of this machine type and is not to scale. Your photo of the open lid shows the real thing.

        Breaker labels are shifted from the drawing

        The wire tags under each breaker show what it really feeds. Cabinet QF2 carries X1/Y1/Z1, which the drawing calls QF3. Cabinet QF3 carries X2/Y2/Z2, drawn as QF4. Cabinet QF4 carries control wire 1, drawn as QF2. Use the table above, and have an electrician correct the stickers or drawing. I read the ratings from a photo, so confirm them on the breakers.

        2.05 kW is not your supply size

        That figure is the press alone: 0.75 kW for each screw, and the remaining 0.55 kW is probably the mixer. The separator motor alone is 4 kW. Its 13.82 A rating sits inside the 12–18 A overload range, and the sludge pump uses that same range, so expect a similar size pump. Size the supply from everything connected.

        Gearbox oil, from the Chinese stickers

        Open the vent cap before starting. The press gearbox has been filled with oil, and the sticker says to confirm the fill and open the cap. Check the oil every 3,000 running hours or 6 months, and change it if low or clearly degraded. It lists heavy-duty industrial gear oil VG220 or VG320. These are my translations, so have a Chinese reader or the maker confirm them.

        The motor wiring sticker

        A yellow sticker gives general motor rules. Standard motors shouldn't run on a drive, and motors with a separate fan need the fan wired separately at the voltage on its plate. It says that is usually 380 V, but your plates say 230 V, so follow the plates. A 4 kW motor is delta only, matching the separator plate.

        What the drawings reveal

        Empty polymer does not stop the feed

        The dissolving-tank float (terminals 36/37) sits only in the dosing pump rung, and a dosing trip FR4 drops only KM4. The sludge pump keeps running, so raw undosed sludge can go into the press with only the fault lamp to warn you. Watch the polymer tank, or have a PLC act on the fault signal. A float going low gives no lamp or signal at all on these drawings.

        Drive switches still matter in Auto

        SA4 SA5 SA6 only work in Manual. SA11 and SA12 sit after the point where the Manual and Auto paths join, so a drive switched off stays off in Auto too. If a screw won't start, look there first.

        Auto stop is not an instant stop

        Auto stop drops KA5. Feed, polymer and mixer stop at once. The screws stay latched through their own contacts until KT2 times out. Turning SA2 out of Auto skips that and kills the screws immediately, which leaves sludge in the barrel.

        Float terminals look jumpered

        Yellow jumper wires sit at the end of the terminal strip, right after the P terminals, where sheet 6 places 31/32 and 36/37. If those are the jumpers, the pumps will start with no floats, but nothing protects them from running dry. Confirm this, then replace each jumper with its float before service. The demo's low-tank buttons show how the circuit acts once floats are wired.

        Manual feed has no high-level cutoff

        LVS1 sits only on the Auto branch, so the electrode rods can't stop KM3 in Manual. Someone has to watch the level. In Auto, sludge buildup on the rods can cause a false full reading, which the manual lists as a cause of a stopped pump.

        A drive fault only stops that drive

        KA20 blocks KM11 and KA21 blocks KM12. The other shaft, the feed and the polymer carry on. Those fault relays also close a shared signal to terminal P4, labelled "Mouse Fault" on the drawing, which looks like a translation slip for a general fault. The drive wiring uses its R1B and R1C terminals, normally the contact that closes on a fault or loss of drive power, so both drive fault lamps may also light whenever the press breaker is off.

        The other machine: the separator

        Your second machine looks like the separator on this panel. Sheet 5 labels its level rods "Solid-Liquid Separator", and the door calls it "Solid liquid equilibrium". It's a different kind of machine. The press uses polymer and squeezes water out of sludge. This one strains raw liquid through a steel screen, with no polymer, and then a screw carries the caught solids away. Its labels are on the photos, but I have no manual or nameplate for it, so the working description is my reading.

        How it runs

        The submersible sewage pump KM6 sends liquid to the water inlet at the top rear. It enters an open trough behind the screen under a welded box, which likely calms the flow. It then spills over the lip and runs down the tilted wedge-wire screen. Liquid drops through the fine slots into the chamber behind and leaves by the filtrate port. Solids stay on the face of the screen and slide down to the screw trough, whose perforated lining lets more liquid drain out.

        The main motor KM5 turns a screw along the trough, carrying solids into the enclosed end housing and out. The vibrator KM7 pulses on timer KT3 to help shake solids free.

        In Auto, the pump only runs while the main motor runs and level relay LVS2 allows it. That means the screw is moving before any liquid arrives. Sheet 5 shows rods E4 to E6 for that level relay, but I can't see them in the photos, so confirm which tank they belong in. The main motor has no drive or speed dial on the drawings, so it runs at one fixed speed.

              Tuning it

              After commissioning, the manual says routine running should need nothing beyond replenishing polymer. It does say to check the sludge regularly, and if the concentration swings by about 10% or more, the cake and throughput will change enough to need adjustment.

              To do thisDo thisWatch for
              Raise throughputSpeed up the screws and feed more through the level adjustment pipeWith the plate gap unchanged, sludge can build up, overload the motor and wear the rings and shaft faster
              Lower throughputSlow the screws and reduce the feed through the level pipeToo much water in the barrel if the screws are too slow for the feed
              Recover from wetter cake when sludge thinsFeed more sludge to restore the solids load and barrel pressureKeep the level at or below the high mark, H position, and keep the sludge flow continuous
              Set the back pressure plateAdjust the gap, then tighten the fixing boltsNever below 4 mm

              Don't let the feed sit so high that the level keeps hitting the top rod. The manual warns that frequent stop-start operation shortens pump life and makes cake moisture and throughput unstable.

              Troubleshooting

              This summarizes the maker's manual, which uses awkward translations. "Alum flower" means floc, and "liquid medicine" or "polymer drugs" means polymer solution.

              ProblemCheck, in order
              Won't run in AutoMode switch, E-stop, tripped overloads, drive errors, and any abnormal state at the polymer system or sludge tank. Also check the sludge tank level.
              No sludge reaching the mixing tankPump failure, air in the pump, blocked or worn impeller, tank already overfull, buildup on the electrode rods, closed valve or blocked line.
              No cake coming outSludge getting into the barrel, blocked pipe to the barrel, floc size, and a back pressure gap that is too tight. Solids can also leak out through the rings when floc is poor.
              Wet cake, small flocsSludge too thick (reduce feed), wrong pH for your polymer, changed polymer concentration, weak or blocked dosing, debris around the weir or level pipe.
              Wet cake, large flocsSludge too thin (raise feed), changed polymer concentration, debris in the metering tank. Then check for overdosing.
              Signs of too much polymerThick sludge around the feed pipe or stuck in ring gaps, poor filtering, viscous filtrate, or drier cake with rising motor current.
              High solids in the filtrateToo much feed, or screws too slow.
              Leaking from a seamToo much feed, screws too slow, or poor floc.
              Moving rings not movingWorn rings. Contact the maker or agent.
              No sprayClosed water valves, clogged sprinkler head, timer on-time at 0 (set above 20 seconds), failed solenoid valve, spray switch or supply.
              Sludge won't discharge after motor workMotor running backward. Cut the power and have the wiring checked. The manual warns that reverse running can damage the machine.

              Resetting a tripped overload

              Set the mode switch to Stop first, because the machine could start and injure someone when the relay resets. Turn off main power, fix the cause, press the blue RESET button on the overload (the manual says white, but yours are blue, with a red STOP), then return to your mode. A very hot relay may need to cool first. If it keeps tripping, stop and contact the maker or agent.

              Clearing a drive error

              Set the mode switch to Stop, fix the cause, reset the drive as its own manual directs, then return to your mode. The press manual mentions a program or reset key, but your ATV320 has an ESC key and a green dial.

              The manual is written for a whole model series and names parts differently from your panel. My matches are COS-1 to SA2, EMS to SB1, OL-0 to the fault lamps, INV to U1 and U2, WL-1 to H1, and TLR-3 to KT1. It also mentions a 24-hour timer, TS-1, which isn't on your drawings.

              Care and warranty

              Daily checks

              Motor running normally, with no strange noise or vibration. Plate gap suitable, and cake moisture steady. Normal filtrate solids. No buildup around the metering tank weir, the horizontal tube or electrodes. Good floc forming.

              Periodic checks

              Cabinet lamps, motor heat and current, timers and drives running to their settings, drive display, moving rings moving, filtrate leaks, solenoid valve operation and leaks, metering tank feed amount, and loose bolts, pipes and valves.

              Idle more than a week

              Use 2 to 3 days if your sludge dries easily, because dried sludge can damage the machine on restart. Drain and wash the mixing tank, running the mixer as it drains. Open the back pressure plate fully and run the screws in Manual for 1 hour. Wash the barrel, then turn off the main power.

              Idle more than 3 months

              Do all of the above. Keep the cabinet door closed and the room air moving to prevent rust. Run the machine in Manual every 3 months to keep the cabinet relays from rusting.

              Wear parts

              The manual's 300 model, which should cover your PJDL-302, lists about 20,000 running hours for dewatering-section moving rings and 50,000 for the screw shaft. These are approximate and are not warranty periods. Keep a log of running hours.

              Warranty

              12 months from the shipment date, so check your shipping papers. The nameplate says 2026.03, so it may run out around March 2027. Consumables are excluded: moving rings, screw shaft and nut, bearings, solenoid valve, baffles, stickers, panel lamps and fuses. So are unauthorized disassembly or modification, running beyond spec and repairs at other shops.

              Before first use, the warranty terms require indoor storage out of rain and leaks, at −10 to 40 °C and below 85% humidity with no condensation. Keep it away from corrosive gas and salt, protect it from nearby construction, and don't connect power or store water or sludge in it.

              Before anyone works on it

              The E-stop is not isolation

              On the drawings it only breaks the control circuit. The drives, cabinet fan and Power lamp all stay powered, and the Power lamp staying lit is expected. Lock out the supply before opening covers or reaching into the cabinet.

              Green is a live wire here

              The cabinet label marks phases A yellow, B green and C red, with PE on a yellow label and yellow-green terminals. The supply leads match, and so do the screw motor fan cables, which use yellow, green and red conductors. In US wiring, green usually means ground, so a US electrician could easily make a dangerous mistake. The motor cables use black, blue and brown, with yellow-green for ground. Point this out to anyone working in the cabinet, and consider relabeling.

              The drives hold a charge

              The label on each Altivar drive says to remove all power and wait 15 minutes before servicing. Follow that even with the breakers open.

              Moving parts under the covers

              The machine carries a pinch warning at the drive end and a goggles warning on the tank. The manual says to turn off the power before cleaning the screw body. In Auto, the level rods can restart the pumps with no one at the panel, and in Remote a PLC can start the press.

              Polymer and sludge

              Polymer spills turn floors extremely slick, and sludge carries its own exposure risks depending on its source. Get the SDS for your polymer and treat the source of the sludge as part of the hazard review.

              What's still open

              Now confirmed

              All six drawing sheets are read. The manual and your tank photos confirm the back pressure plate, metering tank and mixing-tank rods. Your close-ups settle the timer labels, drive model, overload models, separator motor, press gearbox and vibrator wiring.

              KA1 and KA10: partly answered

              On the drawings, KA1 sits between wires 2 and 12 and feeds the press controls. KA10 sits between wires 2 and 61 and feeds the separator controls. Neither relay is on the rail or has a coil on any sheet. Your close-up shows the KA11 and KA12 sockets tagged wire 2 where the drawing says 61, so KA10 appears to have been left out on purpose and bypassed. KA1 may be the same, but the tags on the back of SA2 are hidden in your photos. With power locked out, an electrician can confirm both with a continuity test from wire 2. The demo assumes both circuits are closed. Ask the maker whether these relays had a safety job.

              Still my best reading

              The two float jumpers, the job of each electrode rod, the blurred port labels, the bottom valve and side flange, the box on the screen, and the end housing. Check the drive fault-lamp behavior against the ATV320 manual, because I inferred it from the terminals used.
